_about: H74: the get-started tutorial. The call page shows these pieces on its real screens (the question mark at the top left); the demo call (app/tour.py) reads the same text, so both say the same. Demo content only: nothing here is anyone's real life. {donna}, {pepper} and {moneypenny} become the names of this HQ's agents. H208 (25 October 2026): rewritten in plain words, with getting HQ running (the phone, a server, two HQs, the Mac app, updates) and every feature from the changelog it was missing.
intro: HQ is your own office, with a team in it. You call them, and they don't just talk back: they write things down, plan your days and get work done while you're away. Pick a piece below to see where things are, or try a demo call and ask whatever you want.
demo_note: Demo: everything in this tutorial is made up. Nothing you tap here changes your HQ, and nothing is saved.

pieces.title: Call your team
pieces.line: Who to call, and how a call goes

steps.title: Pick who you call
steps.text: {donna} is the quick one. Your day, your list, your mail, small jobs. {pepper} takes her time. Call her to plan, to think something through, or to talk about the bigger picture. {moneypenny} looks after the building of HQ with the team. They each have their own voice and their own week, and now and then something from their day comes up, like with a colleague.

steps.title: Tap to call
steps.text: One tap and she picks up. Talk like you would on the phone. You can cut in any time, and she stops talking.

steps.title: Call me back, or call me later
steps.text: Say "hang up and call me back" and she does. The app starts fresh and she calls you straight back, on the same call. You can also agree a time: "call me at three", or "call me when my appointment starts". Your phone then shows "{pepper} is calling", and one tap picks up. She already knows what it's about. If you miss it, {donna} tells you in her texts.

items: Call me at three about the report, okay?
Will do. I'll call you at three.

steps.title: Take it back
steps.text: Said something you didn't mean, or she heard you wrong? Cancel takes back what you just said, before she does anything with it. She asks once to make sure.

steps.title: Mute, or hold to talk
steps.text: Tap this button to mute yourself. Hold it down to talk for as long as you want, pauses and all. Let go and she answers.

steps.title: What she's doing
steps.text: This line tells you: listening, thinking or talking. While she thinks you hear a soft tick, so it's never just silence.

items: Three things. The dentist at ten, a call with Alex at two, and the report you wanted done before Friday.

steps.title: Hang up by saying bye
steps.text: You don't have to press anything to end a call. Say bye, "that's it, see you later" or "cheers", and she says goodbye and hangs up. Her goodbye goes with what you're doing next, like the appointment that's coming up. Say something right after and the call goes on.

pieces.title: Calls with more than one
pieces.line: Hand over, or bring someone in

steps.title: Hand the call over
steps.text: Calling {donna} but it's really something for {pepper}? Say "give me {pepper}". {donna} hangs up the normal way, notes and all, and {pepper} picks up right away, knowing what was said.

items: Give me {pepper}, I want to plan my week.

steps.title: Bring someone in
steps.text: Want both on the line? Say "bring in {pepper}" and it's a three-way call. Bring in one more and it's four. The one who joins says hi in her own voice. The screen shows everyone in their own colour.

steps.title: Who answers
steps.text: With more than one on the line, the one you talk to answers. Start with her name, "{pepper}, what do you think?", or end with it. Talking about someone doesn't count, so "what do you think of {moneypenny}'s idea?" goes to whoever you asked. A plain "yes" goes to the one who spoke last.

pieces.title: The chat, and typing
pieces.line: Read back what was said, or type when you can't talk

steps.title: What was said
steps.text: The chat shows the whole call as text while it happens. Lists and bold words show up there, but she never reads the marks out loud.

steps.title: Type instead of talking
steps.text: On a train or in a library? Type in the chat and she answers out loud and in the chat. After a call, Call back and continue picks up where you left off.

items: Remind me to buy coffee tomorrow
Done. I'll text you tomorrow morning at nine.

steps.title: A quick yes
steps.text: She asks for your yes before some things. With nothing typed, hold the grey Send button, slide up onto Yes and let go. That sends a yes without typing a word.

steps.title: Links you can tap
steps.text: When she gives you a web link, it opens with one tap: in the call's chat, in past calls and in {donna}'s chat. The call keeps going in the meantime. She never reads a link out loud.

steps.title: Turn her voice off
steps.text: Turns her voice off and on again, for when you'd rather read. She keeps answering in the chat.

pieces.title: Your to-do list, the Eisenhower way
pieces.line: Everything to do, sorted by what really matters

steps.title: One list for everything
steps.text: Everything you have to do goes here, in four boxes: important or not, urgent or not. Important but not urgent comes first. That's where the things are that really move your life forward, and they're the first to get pushed aside when you don't watch them.

steps.title: You just talk
steps.text: A list like this is normally a lot of admin. In HQ you just say it on a call or in a text, and it lands in the right box, in your own words. When something's done or you let it go, it moves, with a line so you can look back later.

items: Learn to cook three new dishes · Plan the summer trip
Pay the tax bill by Friday

steps.title: Working with it
steps.text: Tap a box to see its list, and an item to see everything about it. Tick it off, move it, let it go, rename it, add one yourself, or start a call about it. Drag the dots at the start of a row to move it up or down. Undo puts the last change back.

steps.title: Planned, or not yet
steps.text: On an item, Plan in a block picks the block in your calendar where it gets done, from the coming two weeks. One block can hold more than one item, and on a call you just say which block. The item then shows that block's day and time, also when the block moves. The filter on a list shows everything, only what's planned, or only what isn't yet.

steps.title: Things that come back
steps.text: Some things come back, like a tax return every quarter or checking the rent each month. On an item, Comes back sets how often. Tick it off and it's back on its own list by itself, with its next date. On a call, just say it repeats. Let it go and it stops.

steps.title: Groceries
steps.text: The groceries have their own list. Add a few at once, one per line or with commas. Tick one when it's in your basket and it goes to a Ticked off list underneath, A to Z. One tap puts it back on the list for next time.

pieces.title: Texts with {donna}
pieces.line: Reminders, heads-ups, and texting her yourself

steps.title: Her own text line
steps.text: {donna} texts you reminders at the time you asked, and a heads-up when something needs you. You can text her back here like in any chat app, and she does what you ask. Allow notifications on your phone and her texts show up on your lock screen.

items: Morning. Dentist at ten, leave by half nine.
Thanks! Move my gym to tonight?

steps.title: Nudge me until it's done
steps.text: Something you keep putting off? Ask her to keep nudging you until it's done. She decides how often, more when it matters or a deadline is close, never at night. Say done and she stops. Say later and she leaves it until the next morning.

steps.title: A text when it starts
steps.text: Ask her to text you when an appointment starts, or a few minutes before. Only the ones you pick get one, and they show a bell in your calendar. She also does reminders outside the calendar, like "remind me at three to call the bank".

steps.title: Let me know when
steps.text: Waiting for a parcel? Say "let me know when it's delivered" and she texts you every update from your mail, until it's there or a week has gone by. It works for the weather too: "let me know if it rains later today". She texts you when it ends as well.

steps.title: Her own notes
steps.text: {donna} keeps a short list of her own, under your quick notes: things she's keeping an eye on, the nudges that are open, and what she's waiting for. Now and then, only when it's worth it, she texts you about one of them.

pieces.title: Your calendar
pieces.line: Your days at a glance, planned on a call

steps.title: Your days
steps.text: Your Google Calendar inside HQ: today and the two weeks ahead. Ask on a call to plan your week, move something or block time, and she does it. The calendar stays open on a call too, so you can look while you talk.

steps.title: Notes and calls on an appointment
steps.text: Tap an appointment to see it, write a quick note on it, or start a call about it. Your own appointments she just changes. Anything with other people in it, she asks you first.

steps.title: Done, or an X
steps.text: Every appointment has a check for done and an X for didn't happen as planned. They're kept in HQ only, nothing moves in your Google Calendar. At the end of the week you look back on a call: what got done, what got an X, and what keeps slipping.

steps.title: The five kinds, in colour
steps.text: Give an appointment a colour in Google Calendar and HQ knows what kind it is. Money makers are yellow: what brings new money in. Client delivery is green: the work someone already pays for. Admin essentials are red. CEO time is blue-green: working on your business and your life. Cup fillers are purple: what fills you up again. Grey is a block you haven't decided on yet. The row of kinds on top lets you hide or show one with a tap, and Edit gives a kind your own name or colour. Google itself isn't changed.

items: Date night · grey, not set yet

steps.title: Travel to an appointment
steps.text: An appointment away from home gets its trip by public transport, once HQ knows where it is: from its place in the calendar, or a friend's address you gave once. It starts from home, or from where you were just before. In the hours before, HQ watches the live train, bus and tram info, and {donna} texts you when your train is cancelled, late or on another platform, with a 9292 link to plan again. Tap Travel on the appointment to turn it on or off. Ask on a call how to get somewhere and you get a 9292 link that plans for the time you leave, with any news about the stops at both ends, like a closed stop or a replacement stop.

items: Train from the station near home, there 13:39

pieces.title: Driving to appointments
pieces.line: By car, with the traffic, on your own maps key

steps.title: Driving to an appointment
steps.text: If you drive, a trip can go by car instead. HQ works out how long the drive takes with the traffic, and when you need to leave. From two hours before, it keeps an eye on the traffic. {donna} texts you when it's time to go, and again if the drive gets ten minutes longer or shorter. It opens in Google Maps. This one is off until you turn it on.

items: Leave by 13:15: 35 minutes by car, 8 of it traffic

steps.title: Your own maps key
steps.text: The traffic comes from a maps service, and HQ doesn't come with a key for it. You make your own once, and it stays on your computer. Two kinds work. Google Maps asks for a card, but its free monthly use covers one person's trips many times over. TomTom is free and needs no card. Pick either one, the next two steps show how.

steps.title: A Google Maps key, step by step
steps.text: 1. Go to console.cloud.google.com and sign in with your Google account. 2. At the top, make a new project, called HQ for example. 3. Open Billing and add a card (Google asks for it; the free use covers HQ). Under Budgets and alerts, set a small budget, like 5 euros, so you hear about it if anything ever costs money. 4. Open APIs and Services, Library, search for Routes API, and press Enable. 5. Open APIs and Services, Credentials, Create credentials, API key. 6. Press Edit on the new key: under API restrictions pick Restrict key, tick only the Routes API, and Save. 7. Copy the key. It starts with AIza.

steps.title: Or TomTom, free without a card
steps.text: 1. Go to developer.tomtom.com and press Register. 2. Fill in your name and email, and confirm the email they send you. 3. Sign in. Your dashboard already has a key on the Keys page. 4. Copy it. The free plan gives 2,500 looks a day. HQ uses about a dozen per trip and never more than 150 a day.

steps.title: Paste it in
steps.text: Open Settings, What HQ helps you with, and turn on Driving to appointments. A box shows up under it: paste your key and press Save. It's kept on this computer only, never in your files and never uploaded. Running two HQs? Paste it on both. Forget takes it off again. Never say or type your key on a call or in a text.

steps.title: On each appointment
steps.text: Open an appointment away from home and tap Travel. With only driving on, every trip goes by car. With public transport on too, a trip starts by public transport and Go by car instead switches it. Or just say it on a call: go by car to the dentist.

pieces.title: Quick notes
pieces.line: Jot something down for later

steps.title: A quick note
steps.text: A thought you don't want to lose? Write it here. The next call can read your notes, so you can say: let's go through my notes. Cleared one by mistake? Tap Undo right after, or later ask on a call to bring it back: nothing you clear is lost.

items: Ask about the new running shoes
Idea: a picnic in the park

steps.title: Feedback for HQ
steps.text: Found a bug, or wish HQ did something? In the notes, tap Feedback, type it and Send. Tick It's a bug when something doesn't work. It goes straight onto the planning of the people building HQ, and next to what you sent you see what happens with it: received, looked at, planned, being built, done, or not doing it.

pieces.title: Past calls
pieces.line: Every call kept, to read back or carry on

steps.title: Every call kept
steps.text: Every call is saved as text. Open one and it starts at the end, like a chat. Scroll up for the start. Read it back, or tap Continue this call and she picks up where you left off, knowing what was said.

pieces.title: The mail check
pieces.line: HQ reads your new mail every hour

steps.title: Every hour, quietly
steps.text: Every hour HQ reads your new mail and keeps only what might need you. The very important things, like a bill with a date or someone waiting for your answer, you hear at the start of every call until you say it's sorted. HQ never sends mail. Drafts at the most, and you send them yourself.

items: Your parcel is on its way

steps.title: Check more often for a while
steps.text: Waiting for something important? Say "check my mail more often until tonight", or for a few hours, or until Friday. HQ then looks every fifteen minutes, and goes back to once an hour by itself when the time's up.

steps.title: Tidy your mail
steps.text: Ask {donna} to tidy up: mark mail read, archive it, star it, or put a label on it. She makes and renames labels too. The trash only when you ask for exactly that.

steps.title: Sorted from now on
steps.text: Want a kind of mail sorted from now on, like all your receipts in one label? {donna} gives you two ways. She walks you through making a real Gmail filter, step by step. Or you agree a sorting rule with her, and the hourly mail check puts new mail in its label for you. You can see your rules, and stop one any time.

pieces.title: Weather and rain
pieces.line: The weather at a glance, a text before the rain

steps.title: The weather
steps.text: The weather where you are. Tap it for more: the next hours, today and tomorrow, and the rain radar for the next two hours. A yellow, orange or red mark means there's an official weather warning, and the full warning is in there too.

steps.title: Rain while you're out
steps.text: When you wake up, {donna} tells you if it'll rain while you're out today. Turn on the rain alert and she also texts before a shower would catch you outside, and keeps following it as it moves. While you sleep, she says nothing.

steps.title: Let me know between 2 and 6
steps.text: Going out at a time that's not in your calendar? Tell her "let me know between 2 and 6", once or every day, and she watches the rain for those hours.

pieces.title: Your own news
pieces.line: Only the topics and sources you pick

steps.title: Your own newspaper
steps.text: News shows only what you asked for: your topics, from the sources you picked, without the noise. It's read about every hour and kept apart from your mail.

steps.title: Set it up in a short call
steps.text: The first time, tap Set up your news. It's a short call about what you want to hear about, what to leave out, and where from. She suggests free sources and checks them. Change it the same way whenever you want.

items: Two science sites, one local paper

steps.title: Read it here
steps.text: Tap an item to read it inside HQ, with its source under it. A dot on the button means there's something new since you last looked.

pieces.title: The team works while you're away
pieces.line: Agree work on a call, hang up, it gets done

steps.title: Give it to the team
steps.text: On a call you can agree a bigger piece of work: build something, sort something out, look something up. Say "give it to the team". You hang up, and your computer does it by itself, one piece at a time.

steps.title: See how far it is
steps.text: The Status page shows what's being done right now and which step it's on, what's waiting, what's planned for later, and how much of your Claude usage is left.

items: Research three summer trips, step 2 of 3

steps.title: Plan it for later
steps.text: Work doesn't have to start right away. On a call, plan it for a day and a time, like tonight at ten, or let it repeat, like every night or every Friday. Give it the priority tag and when its time comes it goes first, ahead of the work that's waiting. A job that's already running is never stopped for it.

steps.title: The usage lines
steps.text: Your Claude plan has a 5-hour limit and a weekly limit. The team stops at a line on each bar, so there's always some left for you. By default the line moves up through the window, so the team doesn't use it all early on. You can also fix a line at a number of your own, on the Status page or by asking on a call.

steps.title: See where the usage goes
steps.text: Each usage bar shows in colours where the work should land: the team's work, what's planned once, and what repeats. Under the 5-hour bar, Show the next 20 hours opens up the windows after this one. Under the weekly bar, Show the whole week opens up today and the six days after it, each with what lands that day and where the line stands. The day the week resets shows twice: up to the reset, and the new week starting again from 0%.

items: +0.3% of the week, the team's work
+3% of the week, the planned bug sprint

steps.title: A paused job
steps.text: If a job uses far more than expected, about four times its estimate, the team pauses it and {donna} tells you. On the Status page, or on a call, you say carry on or stop. Nothing big runs away without you knowing.

steps.title: When something goes wrong
steps.text: When something in HQ stops working, it shows under Incidents on the Status page and {donna} texts you, and again when it's back. A watchdog brings most things back by itself. A job that keeps failing waits for you instead of trying forever.

pieces.title: The planning and the sprint
pieces.line: Ideas first on the planning, then built in a sprint

steps.title: The planning
steps.text: Every bigger idea goes on the planning first, in your own words, so nothing gets lost. Once a week, at your sprint planning, you pick what the team builds next.

steps.title: Rank the planning
steps.text: Every open item gets an estimate by itself: about how long it takes and how much of your usage. On a call, give items their place: "make the feedback button number one", or "put it third". A new item has no place until you give it one, so the others keep theirs.

items: Recipes with the groceries, about 25 min

steps.title: Must, Should, Could, Won't
steps.text: Give each item a tag for the sprint: Must, Should, Could, or Won't this time. Pick it on the item, or say it on a call: "the feedback button is a must". The planning then shows in groups, each in its own colour: Must first, then Should, Could, the ones without a tag, and Won't last.

items: bug: the clock is wrong · Feedback button

steps.title: Bugs before features
steps.text: Your planning keeps bugs and features apart. The tag comes first, so a Must feature stays above a Should bug, and inside each tag the bugs go first. That keeps the tech debt down: shortcuts and unfixed bugs pile up like interest on a loan, until every new change gets slower and riskier. A check that runs every night finds bugs before you do. Ask {moneypenny} about it if your HQ doesn't have one yet.

steps.title: Ready for the sprint
steps.text: Only items marked ready go to the team. Ready means it's written out with you: what done looks like, how to test it, why it matters, what's left out, what it touches, how big it is, what it waits on, and that nothing private goes in. For a small bug: what's wrong, what right looks like, and how to check. Tick Ready on the item, or say "the feedback button is ready". If the words change afterwards, it says Changed since ready until you mark it again. Only when you say so on a call does an unready one go anyway, and then the team knows.

steps.title: Totals for the sprint
steps.text: At the top of Sprint planning, Totals shows how many items there are, about how long they take and how much of your usage. Tap it and it splits into three: not ready yet, ready but not planned, and already planned. The three add up to the total.

items: 20 items, about 5 h, 10% of the week
6 items, about 2 h, 4% of the week
2 items, about 25 min, 1% of the week
28 items, about 7 h 25, 15% of the week

steps.title: Plan the sprint
steps.text: Under Sprint planning, tick the items for this sprint and you see them fall into the coming nights in order. The team works every night from ten in the evening to eight in the morning. Each item shows when it should be done and how much usage it takes, and a line shows where the room runs out. Pick the night it starts and press Plan the sprint. On a call, say "plan these for tonight".

items: the rest waits for the weekly reset

steps.title: Ready before it's built, done when it's done
steps.text: {moneypenny} keeps the planning. She does as much as she can herself, and brings you one whole proposal at a time, as many items as she can: the tags, the open answers, how to split it and in what order. You say yes, change it, or say no. Only what's really yours to decide is left open, with her pick next to it. Every new item she writes, she checks right away, so you can mark it ready on the spot. When something's built she checks it first: it does what was asked, the old checks still pass, new checks are added, and the tutorial and what's new are updated. Then you try it yourself.

pieces.title: Settings
pieces.line: Voices, sound, light or dark, and what HQ helps you with

steps.title: Voices and sound
steps.text: Pick each agent's voice, your microphone, where her voice comes out, and whether you hear the soft thinking sound.

steps.title: Microphone and sound, quickly
steps.text: The microphone button is a shortcut to the same place. Switch to your headphones or another microphone in two taps, also in the middle of a call.

steps.title: What HQ helps you with
steps.text: Every part of HQ is a switch: the calendar, the to-do list, texts, the weather, travel by public transport, the mail check, your news, notes, the team's work, and Life coaching. Turn off what you don't use. Its button goes away and the rest moves up. Driving to appointments starts off, because it needs your own maps key.

steps.title: Light or dark
steps.text: The sun and moon at the top right switches between light and dark in one tap, and HQ keeps it that way on this device. Settings, Look, has System too, to follow your phone or computer again.

steps.title: Free
steps.text: Free is plain Claude with only the web: none of your files, and nothing is saved. Handy when you want to show HQ to someone without showing your life.

pieces.title: Life coaching
pieces.line: Your long-term vision, one calm session at a time

steps.title: Your vision, layer by layer
steps.text: With Life coaching on, this button opens your map. It goes from the life you want in three to five years, down to this year, a six-week game, your ideal week and this week. Each layer has its checklist: what's answered, what's left for later, and what's still open. You give your vision its own name.

steps.title: One session per layer
steps.text: Start a layer and {pepper} calls about only that one, one question at a time, and writes your answers down in your own words. Short sessions, so nothing drifts off.

steps.title: Check-ins, with a red dot
steps.text: HQ keeps the moments to look back: every week, at the end of a game, and a bigger check-in every eight weeks, in step with the games. When one is due, the button gets a red dot. There's also a chat with {pepper} just for life coaching.

pieces.title: Your six-week game
pieces.line: One simple game you can win, six weeks at a time

steps.title: A game you can win
steps.text: In Life coaching you design a six-week game with {pepper}: one simple thing, like moving every day. Once it's set up, this button shows where you are, the win line, and how far along you are.

steps.title: Tick it off
steps.text: Tick today off here, or just say it on a call or text {donna}. Add how it felt, or a note, when you want. {donna} can nudge you in the evening if today's tick isn't in yet.

steps.title: Look back and keep it
steps.text: Every week you look back on it, and at the end there's a short debrief: was it fun, was it useful, what did you learn. Past games are kept, so you can open them again.

pieces.title: HQ on your phone
pieces.line: Call your computer from anywhere

steps.title: Nothing to install on the phone
steps.text: HQ runs on your computer, or on a server. Your phone just calls it. It reaches your computer privately through Tailscale, a free app, with nothing open to the internet.

steps.title: Connect it, step by step
steps.text: 1. Install Tailscale on your computer and on your phone, and sign in on both with the same account. 2. On the phone, open the address your Claude gave you after the install in Safari. It ends in .ts.net:8443. 3. Allow the microphone. That's it, you can call.

steps.title: Put it on your home screen
steps.text: In Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen. HQ's icon, the house, lands next to your other apps and opens like an app. Opened from there, {donna}'s texts can show up on your lock screen once you allow notifications. The Status page has its own address: the same, ending in :8444.

pieces.title: HQ on a server
pieces.line: Always on, also when your laptop is closed

steps.title: Why a server
steps.text: A laptop goes to sleep. A small server never does, so the team keeps working at night and your mail keeps getting checked while your laptop is closed. HQ runs on a Linux server just like on a Mac. Everything works there, except what's about a laptop, like the battery and the lid.

steps.title: Getting it there
steps.text: The steps are the same as on a Mac: install Claude Code on the server, get HQ, and ask Claude to install everything. It tells you plainly what's missing and the line to fix it. You then call it from your phone or laptop through Tailscale, the same way.

pieces.title: Two HQs: main and backup
pieces.line: Your laptop and a server, working as one

steps.title: One main, one backup
steps.text: Have HQ on your laptop and on a server? They can work as one. The main one does the work: the team, the mail check, the planned jobs. The backup takes your calls too and passes anything you agree on to the main one. Your files are the same on both within seconds.

steps.title: Which one is main
steps.text: A small pill next to the name tells you. A green Main on the main one, and a grey Backup, saying which one is main, on the other. Each Status page also shows whether the other one answers, every minute.

steps.title: When one goes away
steps.text: If the main one goes offline, the backup takes over by itself after five minutes, and hands back when the main one returns. Want to switch yourself? Just say it on a call: make the server main. It switches right away, or as soon as the running job is done.

pieces.title: The Mac app
pieces.line: Everything in one window, with the dog

steps.title: One window
steps.text: On a Mac, HQ can have its own app: the call, the Status page and {donna}'s texts in one window. Ask your Claude to build it for you.

steps.title: The dog
steps.text: At the top of the Mac app sits the watchdog, drawn as a dog. Its mood follows how HQ is doing. When something's off it barks Woof! in red. When a new version is out, it sits by its empty food bowl and barks Update! in green.

steps.title: Talk with the space bar
steps.text: In the Mac app the space bar is your mute button. Tap it to mute. Hold it to talk, and let go to send.

steps.title: Music during a call
steps.text: On a Mac your music turns down during a call. Want it to stay normal? In Settings, set Other sound to Normal. With Bluetooth headphones on, the call then uses the MacBook's own microphone, so your headphones keep their full sound.

steps.title: The lid
steps.text: On a laptop, the Status page has a switch on the lid line. One tap and it keeps working with the lid closed. Tap again and it goes to sleep like normal.

pieces.title: Updates
pieces.line: What's new, and getting it

steps.title: The version number
steps.text: A small grey number on the call page, the Status page and in the Mac app tells you which version you're on. Tap it to see what's new in every version.

steps.title: The Update button
steps.text: HQ looks a few times a day for a new version. When there is one, a small bar shows what's new with an Update button. One tap and it updates and restarts what it needs to, without restarting your computer. A call in progress ends, so tap it when you're off a call. Your own files and what you built yourself are never touched.

pieces.title: Make it yours
pieces.line: HQ is built to grow

steps.title: Your own headquarters
steps.text: This is why HQ was built: so everyone can have their own headquarters, with their own team behind them. What's in it now is what its maker thought most people would want. His own HQ has a lot more, and people testing it have already built their own.

steps.title: Change it, add to it
steps.text: You're not stuck with what you see here. Ask on a call for something new, put it on the planning, and the team builds it into your HQ. What you build stays yours.

steps.title: Updates never break your own
steps.text: What you add yourself is an extension. It lives in your own files, and an update never touches it. After every update HQ checks whether something you added might not fit the new version. If so, a short message says which one, with two buttons: talk it through with {donna}, or send it to the team to fix.

steps.title: Coming soon: shared best practices
steps.text: Ways of working that keep a build stable, like the checks that run every night and fix what broke, written so your own HQ understands them. Turn them on, and your HQ keeps an eye out for them and suggests them itself, so you don't have to be a programmer to avoid the classic mistakes.

facts: HQ runs on your own computer, on your own Claude plan, through Claude Code. Your voice is turned into text on your computer, and her voice is made there too. Only the thinking goes to Anthropic, the same as any Claude chat.
Your phone reaches your computer privately, through Tailscale, with nothing open to the internet. Add the call page to your phone's home screen and it works like an app. There's a Mac app too.
Your own files live in your workspace, a folder of plain text files on your computer. They're never uploaded with HQ, and updates never touch them.

HQ is still being built. One person built it and uses it every day, and now it's shared with friends. The small grey version number shows what's new; an Update button shows up when a new version is out.
The routine is a small helper that runs every minute without Claude, so waiting costs nothing. A watchdog brings things back when they stop.
Things that need your yes, like an appointment with other people in it or anything with your mail, are checked with you first. Mail is never sent.
After a real call, the text of it is saved and the call's notes go in your log, in your own words. Free calls and demo calls are never saved.

Travel on appointments uses open data, free and without a key: the live train, bus, tram and metro info the Dutch transport companies publish (through OVapi), the government's address service, and 9292 links. Driving is its own feature, on your own Google Maps or TomTom key, kept on your computer; HQ doesn't come with a key and counts its looks, at most 150 a day.

When an agent calls you at a time you agreed, it comes as a notification on your phone, not a real phone call: an app like this can't ring like a phone, and HQ uses no paid phone service. One tap on it opens HQ and the call starts.
Running HQ on a server and on a laptop at once is set up by your Claude once both are installed; the steps are in INSTALL.md. Windows has no ready version yet.
